stances.claim: Congress should be allowed only one JBC vote because the Constitution is unambiguous — 'a representative of the Congress' — and granting two votes gives Congress an unfair advantage over the executive and judicial branches, each of which has only one ex officio member.
stances.rhetorical_move: textual-clarity argument: the singular 'a representative' as the dispositive constitutional text, backed by structural-equality principle
stances.confidence: asserted in agreement with the Chavez petition

stances.claim: The Dulay vs JBC ruling's identification of the most senior non-applicant justice as the proper JBC presiding officer is ratio decidendi, not obiter — the issue was specifically raised and resolved in that case, making JBC members' contrary claim legally incorrect.
stances.rhetorical_move: obiter-vs-ratio precision argument: issue-specifically-raised test as the dispositive distinction

notable_anecdotes: CJ Panganiban's first-person account of the 2006 JBC episode: Dean Dimayuga formally proposed reverting to one Congressional vote, but Sen. Pangilinan tabled it claiming only the SC had jurisdiction — while CJ himself could not render his opinion because he would have had to inhibit if the matter came to the Court, creating a catch-22 that left the constitutional defect unresolved for six more years.

CJ Teehankee's original 1987 practice of having one alternating senator/congressman — the historical baseline from which the Pimentel-era bloating departed — used as the constitutional-intent anchor for the one-representative argument.

The Committee on Style oversight: the 1986 Constitutional Commission voted to shift from a unicameral to a bicameral legislature but its Committee on Style failed to update the JBC composition provision accordingly — the textual basis for Pimentel's creative two-vote argument, and the reason the constitutional ambiguity persisted.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban identifies two urgent constitutional problems facing the JBC in selecting the new chief justice. First, the dual-representation issue: the Constitution says 'a representative of the Congress' -- singular -- yet a senator and a congressman currently sit and each cast a full vote, bloating membership to eight from the constitutional seven, with significant implications for the majority-vote threshold (5 of 8 vs 4 of 7). He traces the history: CJ Teehankee's original practice was one alternating representative; under CJ Davide, Sen. Pimentel persuaded the JBC to grant two full votes on the theory that the unicameral legislature premise became obsolete when the Constitutional Commission adopted bicameralism -- but the Committee on Style failed to update the JBC composition provision. In 2006, CJ Panganiban recounts, Dean Dimayuga formally proposed reverting to one vote but Sen. Pangilinan tabled it, and CJ himself could not opine without prejudging the case. Former SolGen Chavez has now filed a formal SC petition -- CJ agrees Congress should have only one vote given the Constitution's clear text and the structural-equality principle (executive and judicial branches each get one). Second, the presiding-officer issue: CJ finds that Dulay vs JBC (July 3, 2012) definitively resolved that the most senior non-applicant justice presides over JBC proceedings, making JBC members' claim that this is only obiter incorrect -- the issue was specifically raised and decided, making it ratio decidendi, additionally supported by RA 296 which devolves CJ duties to the most senior associate justice during a vacancy.
